title: Swarg Bana Sakte Hai
author: Ramdhari Singh "Dinkar"
tagline: Dinkar’s argument that heaven is not a place beyond this life but a just society people can build on earth by choice.

overview.intro: Dinkar’s "Swarg Bana Sakte Hai" ("We Can Make Heaven") is a poem of assertion and exhortation, drawn from the counsel Bhishma gives Yudhishthira after the devastation of the Mahabharata war. Its argument moves through three steps: the earth belongs to no one’s purchase and all who are born on it have equal claims to its gifts; injustice persists because those shares are unequal, and peace cannot be secured while some are denied their rightful happiness; and since the earth holds enough good for everyone, people could make it a heaven if they chose to share. The promised heaven is therefore built by human decision, not awaited in an afterlife.

learningOutcomes: Summarise the poem’s three-step movement from equal rights to injustice to the call for change.
Explain the image of the earth as no one’s purchased slave and what it asserts about human claims.
Discuss why Dinkar links unequal shares of happiness to unrest and conflict.
Interpret the closing claim that heaven can be made on earth, and say what it demands of people.

learn.title: The earth belongs to no one’s purchase

blocks.text: The poem opens with a declaration rather than a description. Addressing Yudhishthira as Dharmaraj, Dinkar asserts that the earth is no one’s purchased slave; everyone born on it has an equal claim to its gifts. The needs he lists are concrete — light, air, room to develop, and freedom from fear. This is not abstraction but a statement about basic entitlements, and it establishes the standard by which everything that follows will be judged.

Notice that the address is to a king who has just presided over a war fought, in part, over a kingdom. Placing the argument in Bhishma’s mouth after the carnage gives it immense weight: the speaker has seen what unequal claims produce, and he is naming the principle that was violated.

items: Obstacles still stand in humanity’s path, blocking the equal enjoyment the opening demands.
Justice and peace cannot be secure while people are denied their rightful share of happiness.
Unequal shares produce suspicion, fear and self-interest rather than harmony.
Instead of community, people accumulate pleasures for themselves — a hoarding that deepens the wrong.
The poem’s diagnosis is therefore moral as much as material: the fault lies in choices, not in the earth.

blocks.text: The middle of the poem is a diagnosis of unrest. Dinkar argues that conflict does not arise from scarcity but from inequality: when some hold more than their share, the rest respond with suspicion and fear, and those who hold respond by accumulating more. The result is a cycle of hoarding and mistrust that no amount of force can settle. Peace, he insists, is impossible while the underlying shares remain unjust.

learn.title: Enough for everyone, if we choose

blocks.text: The poem’s turn is its famous claim: the earth contains enough good for everyone, and people could all be satisfied if they chose to share its benefits fairly. Heaven, in Dinkar’s argument, is not a supernatural destination but a condition of society — just, peaceful, generous — that human beings could produce at once if they willed it. The conditional is crucial: the capacity exists, and what is missing is the choice.

items.text: The earth is no one’s purchased slave.
items.note: A claim about equal entitlement that grounds the whole poem’s moral architecture.

items.text: Until each person’s share of happiness is equal, peace cannot be secured.
items.note: The diagnosis: unrest is produced by unequal shares rather than by an shortage of goods.

items.text: If they so choose, people can make the earth a heaven in a moment.
items.note: The closing exhortation, placing responsibility squarely on human decision.

learn.title: Bhishma, Yudhishthira and the weight of the setting

blocks.text: Reading the poem as counsel after the Mahabharata deepens every line. Yudhishthira has won a kingdom at the cost of his own family; Bhishma lies dying on the battlefield he helped to create. A call for equal shares and an end to hoarding, placed in that mouth, is not abstract idealism but a witness statement from someone who has seen the alternative. The devastation supplies the argument’s evidence.

This setting also explains the poem’s tone, which is urgent and imperative rather than gently persuasive. Dinkar’s diction is emphatic, built on parallel phrases and repeated calls to "all", because the audience is not a seminar but a king — and, by extension, a society being asked to choose.

blocks.caption: The poem’s three-step architecture
rows: The earth belongs to no one; all born on it share its gifts
Personification of the earth, parallel address
Unequal shares produce suspicion, fear and hoarding
Contrast between equal birth and unequal enjoyment
Enough exists; people could make earth a heaven by choice

blocks.text: Dinkar’s chief devices are parallelism and repetition, especially the recurring emphasis on "all", which makes the argument feel like a chorus rather than a lecture. He personifies the earth as an enslaved figure to sharpen the moral outrage, and he contrasts the equality of birth with the inequality of enjoyment to expose the injustice as human-made. Rhetorical questions press the reader toward the conclusion the poem has already reached.

This poem reliably yields questions on the central idea and on the significance of its closing claim. Both are answered by holding the three steps together: equal entitlement, diagnosis of unequal shares, and the conditional promise of a heaven made by choice. Because the poem is argumentative rather than narrative, strong answers state the argument clearly and use the Mahabharata setting to explain its urgency rather than retelling the epic.

items: Frame the central idea as a conditional: heaven is possible, but it requires a choice to share.
Explain why unequal happiness, not scarcity, produces unrest in Dinkar’s diagnosis.
Use the Bhishma-Yudhishthira setting to show the argument is a witness statement, not a slogan.

keyPoints: The poem is framed as Bhishma’s counsel to Yudhishthira after the Mahabharata war.
It opens by asserting the earth is no one’s purchased slave and all who are born share its gifts.
The needs listed are concrete: light, air, room to develop, and freedom from fear.
Justice and peace cannot be secure while people are denied their rightful share of happiness.
Unequal shares produce suspicion, fear and self-interest rather than harmony.
Hoarding pleasures deepens the wrong; the fault is in choices, not in the earth.
The earth holds enough good for everyone, so all could be satisfied by fair distribution.

examFocus: Central idea: a heaven on earth is possible through equal shares and the human choice to share.
Significance of the ending: heaven is conditional on choice, not on fate or the supernatural.
Setting question: Bhishma’s post-war counsel gives the argument the weight of a witness statement.

questions.prompt: Who is the poem framed as speaking to?
questions.explanation: The poem presents Bhishma’s counsel to Yudhishthira on the battlefield, which gives the call for equal shares the weight of a witness who has seen what inequality produces.
questions.commonMistake: The frame is Bhishma to Yudhishthira, not a general address to readers.

questions.prompt: What does Dinkar assert about the earth in the opening?
options: It is no one’s purchased slave and all share its claims
It belongs to those who conquer it
It is exhausted and cannot sustain all
It is a temporary home before heaven
questions.answer: It is no one’s purchased slave and all share its claims
questions.explanation: The earth is described as no one’s purchased slave; everyone born on it has an equal claim to light, air, room to develop and freedom from fear.
questions.commonMistake: The claim is of equal entitlement, not ownership by conquest.

questions.prompt: According to the poem, what prevents justice and peace from being secure?
options: People being denied their rightful share of happiness
questions.answer: People being denied their rightful share of happiness
questions.explanation: Dinkar’s diagnosis is that unrest follows unequal shares: while some are denied their rightful happiness, suspicion, fear and hoarding make peace impossible.
questions.commonMistake: The obstacle is inequality of shares, not a shortage of goods.

questions.prompt: How does the poem define heaven in its closing claim?
options: A just society people can build on earth by choice
A place only the virtuous reach
A kingdom without war but with kings
questions.answer: A just society people can build on earth by choice
questions.explanation: The famous closing asserts that if people choose, they can make the earth a heaven at once — so heaven is a human achievement, conditional on the willingness to share.
questions.commonMistake: It is not an afterlife; the poem relocates heaven into present human decision.

questions.prompt: Which basic needs does Dinkar say all people equally require?
questions.answer: Light, air, room to develop themselves, and freedom from fear.
questions.explanation: These concrete entitlements ground the poem’s opening assertion that the earth belongs to no one and all who are born on it share its gifts equally.
questions.commonMistake: Name the four needs specifically rather than generalising to "everything".

questions.prompt: How does the poem link unequal shares to conflict?
questions.answer: It argues that when some hold more than their share, others respond with suspicion and fear, and the privileged respond by accumulating more, producing a cycle of hoarding and mistrust.
questions.explanation: Dinkar presents unrest as a consequence of distribution rather than of scarcity, so conflict is moral and fixable rather than inevitable.
questions.commonMistake: Show the mechanism — suspicion and hoarding reinforcing each other — rather than stating only that inequality is bad.

questions.prompt: Explain the claim that people can make the earth a heaven, and what it demands.
questions.answer: Dinkar argues that the earth already contains enough good for everyone, so universal satisfaction is possible if its benefits are shared fairly. Heaven, in this poem, is not a supernatural destination but a condition of society — just, peaceful and generous — produced by human decision. The demand the claim places on people is precisely a choice: to abandon hoarding, accept equal shares and treat the earth’s gifts as common entitlement rather than private property. The conditional "if they so choose" is the poem’s moral hinge, because it insists that the only thing missing is the will, not the resources.
questions.explanation: Paraphrase the claim, define the poem’s heaven, then name the demand — the choice to share — so the answer shows what the conditional carries.
questions.commonMistake: Do not present it as a vague optimism; the argument is specifically about distribution and choice.

questions.prompt: Why is the Mahabharata setting significant for the poem’s argument?
questions.answer: Because Bhishma speaks after a war that cost both sides their families, so his call for equal shares is a witness statement grounded in the devastation that inequality produces.
questions.explanation: The setting converts the poem from idealism into testimony: the speaker has seen the alternative to the society he describes, which gives the exhortation its urgency.
questions.commonMistake: Do not retell the epic; explain what the setting does to the argument’s authority.

questions.prompt: Describe the movement of the poem and show how its argument builds to its closing call.
questions.answer: The poem moves in three steps. It opens by asserting that the earth is no one’s purchased slave and that all born on it have equal claims to its gifts — light, air, room to develop and freedom from fear. It then diagnoses why this principle is violated: obstacles still block humanity’s path, and justice and peace cannot be secure while people are denied their rightful share of happiness. Unequal shares produce suspicion, fear and self-interest, and instead of community people accumulate pleasures, deepening the wrong in a cycle of hoarding and mistrust. The poem finally turns to its call: the earth holds enough good for everyone, all could be satisfied if benefits were shared fairly, and if people chose they could make the earth a heaven at once. The argument therefore builds from a claim of equal rights, through a diagnosis of human-made injustice, to a conditional promise whose whole weight rests on the willingness to choose differently.
questions.explanation: Follow the three steps in order, keeping the conditional at the close, so the answer reconstructs the argument rather than quoting fragments.
questions.commonMistake: Do not skip the diagnosis — the middle step is what makes the closing call logical rather than sentimental.

questions.prompt: Do you agree that heaven can be made on earth simply by choosing to share? Discuss.
questions.answer: Dinkar’s claim is moral rather than mechanical, and its strength lies in the word "choose". He is right that the earth’s goods are sufficient and that most suffering follows distribution rather than scarcity — the poem’s diagnosis of hoarding and suspicion still describes the world accurately. But choice is not costless: sharing asks the privileged to give up advantages they have learned to treat as property, and history suggests such choices are made slowly and under pressure. The poem is therefore less a prediction than a standard — it names what a just society would require of us. Reading it as an achievable horizon rather than an instant promise keeps both its urgency and its honesty.
questions.explanation: Take a clear position, acknowledge the accuracy of the diagnosis, then complicate the mechanism — choice is real but costly — before landing on the poem as a standard rather than a guarantee.
questions.commonMistake: Do not reject the poem as naive or accept it as a formula; the discussion lies in what "choose" actually demands.
